title: I'm building a feudal sci-fi strategy game with AI coding agents. The most useful thing I've learned: make the AI prove its fix, not just pass its test
author: Ivaricus
selftext:
Hey! I'm a solo dev making Houses of Veyra, a feudal sci-fi sandbox: Bannerlord-style world map and real-time squad battles, with CK3-style politics on top. It's Godot 4, runs in the browser (phones too), and it's free to play: [https://jonnysoft.itch.io/houses-of-veyra](https://jonnysoft.itch.io/houses-of-veyra)

I direct and design it, and the code is written by AI coding agents (Claude Code now, Codex before it). The art (portraits, map, menu and battle art) is generated with ChatGPT from written briefs. I wanted to share the workflow, because it's what made a project this size possible, and one story from this week that changed how I work.

The setup

 \- A rules file the agent reads every session (CLAUDE.md). It says where things live, how to run the tests, what's flaky, and the rules: every new feature starts as a short plan I approve, work happens in small stages, every change in behaviour gets a focused test, and each stage ends with a checkpoint note and a commit.

 \- Checkpoint notes for each big feature, newest entry at the top. A new session reads them and picks up where the last one stopped, with the numbers, not just "done".

 \- A big headless test suite (225 tests now) that the agent runs in parallel. Plus deliberate bugs: after writing a test, the agent breaks the code on purpose to check the test actually catches it. A surprising number of tests didn't, at first.

 \- Measuring tools instead of guesses. For battles, a tool that fights hundreds of simulated battles and reports what happened. For speed, a script that loads the web build in headless Chrome, throttles the CPU to phone speed and measures frame times.

 \- Art from written specs. Each art slot has a spec (size, style, what it must show) and a ChatGPT prompt file; a converter script imports the results into Godot. The game draws its own placeholder versions until the art arrives, so nothing waits on art.



The story: the fix that passed every test and broke the game

Melee formations in my battles had a bug: lines would meet and then stand around, some soldiers not fighting for 10+ seconds. The agent built a measuring tool, traced the causes, and fixed it over four stages: soldiers left out of a fight now break ranks to find one, and give up targets they can't reach. Idle formations went from 63 battles in 100 to 3. Every test passed.

Stage five of the plan was "prove it": fight 100 battles all the way to the end, before and after, and compare winners against the game's own auto-resolve. That's where it fell apart. The player's side used to win 79 of 100; now it won 38. When the agent bisected the change and traced who downs whom in the first 15 seconds, the cause was clear: the old bug had been hiding a balance problem. With the stall, the enemy's spare soldiers stood idle. With the fix, they all joined the first clash, won it, and the morale losses cascaded through my army.

So 0.1.30 shipped with that part switched off behind a flag, still tested, until the morale system is fixed. Without that last "prove it" stage, I'd have shipped a game where you lose most battles and wouldn't have known why.

My takeaways:

 \- "The tests pass" isn't the finish line. Ask the agent to measure the thing the player feels (here: who wins) before and after.

 \- Make it verify its own tools. While checking the browser speed this week, it found the speed script had been measuring the main menu for weeks, because a menu button had moved. It took screenshots to find out.

 \- Small stages with approval keep the agent from running off. When I let it go long on its own, it drifts into research nobody asked for.

 \- Decisions stay mine. The agent recommends, I pick. Design calls (like "every town starts as a small lordship and villages start free", coming next update) come from me playing the game.

What's in this update: the politics was rebuilt around five pieces (Standing, Influence, Favours, the Court and the Oath), with schemes, and big decisions made by an open vote of the houses with no dice rolls. There's also a painted map, a portrait for every character, auto-resolve, and a ? help button on every screen.

Play free in your browser: [https://jonnysoft.itch.io/houses-of-veyra](https://jonnysoft.itch.io/houses-of-veyra)

I'd love to hear how others structure long projects with agents. How do you keep context between sessions, and how do you catch the "passes the tests, breaks the game" kind of bug?
